Sample Size for AIPE on a Semipartial (Part) Correlation

Source: R/ss_aipe_semipartial_r.R
ss_aipe_semipartial_r.Rd

Takes a planning value of the population semipartial correlation \(\rho_{Y(X \cdot Z_1 \cdots Z_{p-1})}\) (the correlation of \(Y\) with the part of \(X\) that \(Z_1, \ldots, Z_{p-1}\) do not explain, with \(Y\) not residualized), the number of predictors (X and the variables partialed out), and a desired confidence interval width, and returns the smallest sample size at which the interval is expected to be that narrow (accuracy in parameter estimation, AIPE; Kelley & Maxwell, 2003). With assurance it returns, by simulation, the smallest sample size at which the realized interval is that narrow with about the stated probability (the search and the probability reported are both Monte Carlo estimates; see Details).

Usage

ss_aipe_semipartial_r(
  true_r_sp,
  p,
  width,
  which_width = c("Full", "Lower", "Upper"),
  conf_level = 0.95,
  assurance = NULL,
  true_R2_full = NULL,
  G = 20000,
  seed = NULL
)

Arguments

true_r_sp

Population semipartial correlation the sample size is planned for, in \((-1, 1)\). The planner treats this value as the truth; ss_aipe_semipartial_r_sensitivity shows what the plan delivers when the truth (true_r_sp there) differs from the value planned with (supposed_r_sp there).

p

Number of predictors in the regression of Y on X and the variables partialed out, so p - 1 variables are partialed out and p is at least 2. A categorical variable with a levels counts as a - 1 predictors. It is the p of ss_power_R2, ci_R2, and ci_reg_coef: the correlation concerns one predictor of a regression with p predictors. In the notation of a model comparison, \(q\) is the number of predictors removed from the full model to give the restricted model (\(q = p_{full} - p_{restricted}\), the predictors being tested), and the number of variables partialed out is \(p - q\); this correlation concerns one predictor, so \(q = 1\) and \(p - 1\) variables are partialed out.

width

Desired full width of the confidence interval on the semipartial correlation.

which_width

Whether width refers to the "Full" width (default) or the "Lower"/"Upper" half-width.

conf_level

Desired confidence level (default 0.95).

assurance

Optional. The probability that the realized interval is no wider than width. The function returns the smallest sample size, at or above the sample size planned without it, at which the simulated probability is at least assurance (see "The assurance step" in Details). A single number above 0.5 and below 1; when NULL (the default) the plan is for the expected width only and nothing is simulated.

true_R2_full

Population squared multiple correlation of the full model the sample size is planned for, the model with \(X\) and every variable partialed out (true_R2_Y_X in ss_aipe_reg_coef), treated as the truth as true_r_sp is, in \([0, 1]\) and not smaller than true_r_sp squared (a smaller value is refused with an error of class dmar_semipartial_r_incoherent, unless the pair could have come from rounding to two decimals, when the plan proceeds as if true_R2_full were true_r_sp squared and gives a warning of class dmar_semipartial_r_rounded; see var_semipartial_r). When NULL (the default), the plan uses the largest variance over every full-model \(R^2\) that is possible with true_r_sp, so the sample size is sufficient whatever that \(R^2\) is.

G

Number of simulated samples at each sample size the assurance step tries, and in the final estimate of the attained probability; a whole number of at least 100 (default 20000). A smaller value is refused, because the step estimates a probability from these samples and with fewer than 100 its standard error can exceed .05. Used and checked only when assurance is given.

seed

Optional single number. When given, the assurance step is reproducible, and the random number stream of the calling session is left as it was. With NULL (the default) the draws come from the session's current stream. Used only when assurance is given.

Value

A data.frame with the columns term and value and one row per term:

necessary_N

the planned total sample size.

expected_width

the full width of the interval at necessary_N when the two sample values equal the planning values.

true_r_sp, p, width, conf_level

the inputs, with width the width as given.

true_R2_full

the planning value of the full-model \(R^2\); NA when none was supplied.

assurance

the requested probability; present only when assurance was given, as are the next two rows.

assurance_attained

the proportion of G fresh simulated samples of size necessary_N whose interval was no wider than the target. Its Monte Carlo standard error is the attribute assurance_mc_se.

G

the number of simulated samples.

Details

Estimand and interval. The quantity planned for is the population semipartial correlation of \(Y\) with \(X\) given \(Z_1, \ldots, Z_{p-1}\), for independent observations from a multivariate normal population. The interval is the two-sided Wald interval at conf_level, the estimate plus and minus \(z_{1 - \alpha/2} \sqrt{\hat V / (N - p)}\), where \(\hat V\) is the first-order variance below evaluated at the sample semipartial correlation and the sample full-model \(R^2\) (var_semipartial_r with under_null = FALSE). Its limits are not truncated at \(-1\) and \(1\).

Asymptotic variance of the semipartial. Under multivariate normality, to first order, the sample semipartial correlation has variance \(V / N\), with $$V \;=\; (1 - \rho_{sp}^2)^2 \;-\; P_r^2\,(1 - 2 \rho_{sp}^2),$$ where \(\rho_{sp}\) is the population semipartial correlation (true_r_sp) and \(P_r^2\) is the full-model \(R^2\) (true_R2_full) minus \(\rho_{sp}^2\), that is, the squared multiple correlation of \(Y\) with the variables partialed out. This is the first-order variance of Aloe and Becker (2012, Equation 4), which they obtain from Alf and Graf (1999), with \(N - p\) in place of their \(n\): in their notation the numerator is \(P^4 - 2 P^2 + P_{(f)}^2 + 1 - P_{(f)}^4\), with \(P^2\) the full-model and \(P_{(f)}^2\) the restricted-model squared multiple correlation, which equals \(V\) with \(P_r^2 = P_{(f)}^2\). It follows from the delta method variance of the difference between two nested squared multiple correlations (Model A of Olkin & Finn, 1995, for one variable partialed out; Alf & Graf, 1999, for any number; see var_semipartial_r). The planner uses the divisor \(N - p\), as var_semipartial_r does. Inverting for the sample size needed to achieve a target half-width \(w_{1/2}\) at confidence level \(1 - \alpha\): $$N \;=\; p + \Big\lceil z_{1 - \alpha/2}^{2} \cdot V / w_{1/2}^{2} \Big\rceil.$$

Planning without true_R2_full. \(V\) decreases in \(P_r^2\) when \(\rho_{sp}^2 < 1/2\) and increases in \(P_r^2\) when \(\rho_{sp}^2 > 1/2\), so its largest value over every possible full-model \(R^2\) is $$\max\{(1 - \rho_{sp}^2)^2,\; \rho_{sp}^2 (1 - \rho_{sp}^2)\},$$ and the planner uses that value when true_R2_full is NULL. For \(\rho_{sp}^2 \le 1/2\) it is \((1 - \rho_{sp}^2)^2\), the variance when the variables partialed out explain none of the outcome; Algina and Olejnik (2003, p. 317) note, for the squared semipartial correlation, that the required sample size is largest when the squared multiple correlation of the restricted model is zero. A planning value of true_R2_full then gives a smaller sample size. For \(\rho_{sp}^2 > 1/2\) the largest value is \(\rho_{sp}^2 (1 - \rho_{sp}^2)\), approached as the full-model \(R^2\) approaches 1.

Comparison with partial-r planning. The partial correlation \(r_{XY \cdot Z}\) divides the covariance after residualizing both \(X\) and \(Y\) on \(Z\); the semipartial divides after residualizing only \(X\). The semipartial is the natural effect size companion to a standardized regression coefficient: its square equals the \(\Delta R^2\) contributed by \(X\) above and beyond the variables partialed out. See var_semipartial_r for the asymptotic variance, and ss_aipe_partial_r for the partial-correlation analog of this function.

Limits of the plan. The plan is a first-order one. When the returned sample size is small, which happens when \(|\rho_{sp}|\) is large and true_R2_full is near true_r_sp squared, the first-order variance understates the variance of the estimate and the realized intervals are wider than planned; check such a plan with ss_aipe_semipartial_r_sensitivity. The planned sample size is also small when true_R2_full is near 1, for any true_r_sp, and the same check applies: the plan for true_r_sp = .1, p = 4, a width of .20, and true_R2_full = .99 is 12, at which the intervals missed the population value in .13 of 200,000 simulated samples. When \(|\rho_{sp}|\) is above about .9 and the variables partialed out explain some of the outcome, the interval misses more often on one side than the other even with several hundred observations (in one simulated condition, \(\rho_{sp} = .95\), a full-model \(R^2\) of .97, \(p = 2\), and \(N = 395\), it missed in .064 of samples, .051 of them on one side). A plan with true_r_sp = 0 and true_R2_full = 1 is refused, because the first-order variance is zero there and no sample size follows from it.

The assurance step. A plan without assurance makes the interval as narrow as the target when the two sample values equal their planning values; in roughly half of all samples it is wider. With assurance the function looks for the sample size at which the realized interval is no wider than the target with that probability. The width of the interval depends on two statistics, the sample semipartial correlation and the sample full-model \(R^2\), and no closed form for their joint distribution is used here, so the probability is simulated:

  1. What is simulated. Samples of size \(N\) from a multivariate normal population with semipartial correlation true_r_sp and full-model \(R^2\) true_R2_full: \(X\), \(Z_1, \ldots, Z_{p-1}\), and an error \(E\) are independent standard normal, and \(Y = \rho_{sp} X + P_r\, Z_1 + \sqrt{1 - \rho_{sp}^2 - P_r^2}\, E\). Under normality the distribution of the two statistics depends on the population only through \(\rho_{sp}\), the full-model \(R^2\), \(p\), and \(N\) (see ss_aipe_semipartial_r_sensitivity), so this population stands for all of them. The sums of squares and products of the \(p + 1\) independent variables are Wishart with \(N - 1\) degrees of freedom, and the function draws the few entries of that matrix's triangular factor that the two statistics depend on (the Bartlett decomposition) in place of the data.

  2. The interval. From each draw, the sample semipartial correlation and sample full-model \(R^2\) give the half-width \(z_{1 - \alpha/2} \sqrt{\hat V / (N - p)}\), the interval that is planned and that ss_aipe_semipartial_r_sensitivity forms from data.

  3. The search. The simulated probability at \(N\) is the share of G half-widths no larger than the target half-width. Starting from the sample size planned without assurance, the step upward doubles until that share reaches assurance, and a bisection finds the first sample size at which it does, with fresh draws at every sample size tried. The answer is never below the plan without assurance.

  4. The attained probability. The share that chose \(N\) is biased upward by the choice, so assurance_attained is estimated again at the returned \(N\) from G draws that had no part in choosing it. Its standard error, \(\sqrt{A (1 - A) / G}\) with \(A\) that proportion, is the attribute assurance_mc_se.

Plans made this way were checked from data with ss_aipe_semipartial_r_sensitivity in 11 conditions (5,000 simulated data sets each; a Monte Carlo standard error of .003 to .006): the proportion of intervals no wider than the target was .798 to .819 for a requested .80, .854 to .858 for .85, .906 to .908 for .90, and .953 for .95.

The step has properties a closed-form plan does not.

  • The answer has Monte Carlo error. Without seed, two calls can return sample sizes that differ by a few cases (eight unseeded plans at the default G for one condition gave 252 to 254, and 40 seeded plans of each of two other conditions gave 470 to 473 and 306 to 310). The probability at the smallest of those sizes was below the request (.897 and .895 for a requested .90), so a plan is the size at which the probability is about, and not at least, the request. Give seed for a plan that can be reproduced, and report it with G.

  • assurance_attained can fall below assurance by a few of its standard errors, since it is estimated from draws that did not choose \(N\). Its standard error is .003 at the default G and an assurance of .80; in 200 seeded plans the lowest value was .009 below a request of .90. It is an unbiased estimate of the probability at the sample size returned. A larger G narrows both this and the spread of the sample sizes.

  • Without true_R2_full the simulated population is the one the plan without assurance is made for: variables partialed out that explain none of the outcome (\(P_r^2 = 0\)) when true_r_sp squared is at most 1/2, and a full-model \(R^2\) of 1 (\(P_r^2 = 1 - \rho_{sp}^2\), no error term) when it is above 1/2. The second is the limit that gives the largest first-order variance; ss_aipe_semipartial_r_sensitivity refuses a population \(R^2\) of exactly 1, so check such a plan there with a value just below 1 or give true_R2_full.

  • which_width = "Lower" or "Upper" treats width as a half-width, in the assurance step as in the plan.

  • G and seed are checked and used only when assurance is given; without it nothing is drawn and the three rows are absent.

References

Alf, E. F., Jr., & Graf, R. G. (1999). Asymptotic confidence limits for the difference between two squared multiple correlations: A simplified approach. Psychological Methods, 4(1), 70–75. doi:10.1037/1082-989X.4.1.70

Algina, J., & Olejnik, S. (2003). Sample size tables for correlation analysis with applications in partial correlation and multiple regression analysis. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 38(3), 309–323. doi:10.1207/s15327906mbr3803_02

Aloe, A. M., & Becker, B. J. (2012). An effect size for regression predictors in meta-analysis. Journal of Educational and Behavioral Statistics, 37(2), 278–297. doi:10.3102/1076998610396901

Cohen, J., Cohen, P., West, S. G., & Aiken, L. S. (2003). Applied multiple regression/correlation analysis for the behavioral sciences (3rd ed.). Lawrence Erlbaum.

Kelley, K., & Maxwell, S. E. (2003). Sample size for multiple regression: Obtaining regression coefficients that are accurate, not simply significant. Psychological Methods, 8(3), 305–321. doi:10.1037/1082-989X.8.3.305

Maxwell, S. E., Delaney, H. D., & Kelley, K. (2027). Designing experiments and analyzing data: A model comparison perspective (4th ed.). Routledge. (See Chapter 3 on the one-way ANOVA and Chapter 4 on contrasts.)

Olkin, I., & Finn, J. D. (1995). Correlations redux. Psychological Bulletin, 118(1), 155–164. doi:10.1037/0033-2909.118.1.155

Examples

# 1. Plan N so the 95% CI on r_sp (three variables partialed out, so
#        p = 4 predictors) has full width <= 0.15 when the planning
#        value of the semipartial is 0.25, whatever the full-model R^2.
ss_aipe_semipartial_r(true_r_sp = 0.25, p = 4, width = 0.15)
#>  term           value
#>  necessary_N    605  
#>  expected_width 0.150
#>  true_r_sp      0.250
#>  p              4    
#>  width          0.150
#>  conf_level     0.950
#>  true_R2_full   <NA> 
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%

# 2. With a planning value of 0.42 for the full-model R^2, fewer are
#        needed.
ss_aipe_semipartial_r(true_r_sp = 0.25, p = 4, width = 0.15,
                      true_R2_full = 0.42)
#>  term           value
#>  necessary_N    391  
#>  expected_width 0.150
#>  true_r_sp      0.250
#>  p              4    
#>  width          0.150
#>  conf_level     0.950
#>  true_R2_full   0.420
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%

# 3. With an assurance of .80, found by simulation. G = 2000 keeps the
#        example quick; a reported plan deserves the default G = 20000.
#        The last three rows are the request, the proportion of fresh
#        simulated samples that met the width at the returned N, and G.
plan <- ss_aipe_semipartial_r(true_r_sp = 0.25, p = 4, width = 0.15,
                              assurance = 0.80, G = 2000, seed = 113)
plan
#>  term               value
#>  necessary_N        621  
#>  expected_width     0.148
#>  true_r_sp          0.250
#>  p                  4    
#>  width              0.150
#>  conf_level         0.950
#>  true_R2_full       <NA> 
#>  assurance          0.800
#>  assurance_attained 0.804
#>  G                  2000 
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%
attr(plan, "assurance_mc_se")
#> [1] 0.008876486
